title: Revenue, profit and margins
desc: Sales, what’s left after costs, and the margin that tells them apart

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Who keeps more?
cards.situation: Acme sells $100M a year and keeps $20M as profit. Northwind sells $500M and keeps $25M. Which one keeps more of each dollar it sells?

visual.title: Revenue and profit
visual.label: Acme: $100M revenue, $20M profit. Northwind: $500M revenue, $25M profit

options.text: Northwind: it sells five times more
options.feedback: Northwind sells more, but it keeps only 5 cents of each dollar. Acme keeps 20.
Acme keeps four times more of each sale. That share is called the margin.

options.text: The same: both make a profit
options.feedback: Both make a profit, but not the same share of each sale. Acme keeps 20 cents a dollar, Northwind only 5.

cards.title: Sales, profit, margin
cards.text: **[[revenue|Revenue]]** is all the money from sales. **[[profit|Profit]]** is what’s left after every cost. **[[profit-margin|Margin]]** is profit ÷ revenue: how much of each dollar the company keeps.

cards.added: Tap notes written for the Academy (the working for each year’s margin)
cards.title: Sales up, margin down
cards.text: Acme’s sales grew every year. Look at what it kept: margin = profit ÷ revenue.
cards.foot: Sales +50%, profit −25%. Each sale earns less, maybe from price cuts or rising costs. That’s a warning sign.

cards.title: Bigger is better?
cards.myth: More sales means a better company.
cards.reality: Sales are only the start. What counts is how much the company keeps, and whether that is growing or shrinking.
cards.rule: check revenue, profit and margin together, over a few years.

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Work out the margin
cards.q: Northwind sold $200M last year and made $30M profit. What’s its margin?

options.feedback: Profit ÷ revenue: Northwind keeps 15 cents of every dollar it sells.
$30M is the profit, not the margin. Divide it by the revenue.
That’s revenue ÷ profit, upside down. Margin is profit ÷ revenue.
85% is the part of each dollar that went on costs. The margin is the part the company keeps.

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Fast growth, thin margin
cards.q: Acme’s sales grew 30% this year, but its margin fell from 18% to 9%. What should you think?

options.text: Great year: sales are what count
options.feedback: Sales grew, but the margin halved. Each dollar of sales now keeps half as much profit.

options.text: A warning: each sale earns much less
options.feedback: The margin halved, so each dollar of sales keeps half as much profit. Growth like that is worth a closer look.

options.text: Margins don’t matter for big firms
options.feedback: Margins matter for every company. A falling margin means each sale earns less, whatever the size.

options.text: The company is about to go bust
options.feedback: One weaker year doesn’t mean bust. It’s a warning to watch, not a verdict.

cards.headline: You can tell sales from profit.
lines: Revenue is sales, profit is what’s left.
Growing sales with shrinking margins is a warning.
